meta.title: video-lens: measure video in Claude Code
meta.description: A Claude Code skill that measures video on your Mac: UI animation timing and easing as CSS, scene cuts, on-screen text and speech with timestamps. Nothing is uploaded.

nav.github_aria: Open the video-lens repository on GitHub

hero.pitch: Measures video instead of eyeballing it, so Claude can answer when, for how long and how. Everything runs on your Mac.
hero.lede: Claude cannot watch video. video-lens measures it frame by frame, hands Claude numbers and text first, and shows images only where a look is needed.
hero.strip_aria: Two rows of 30 frames. At 60 fps a 300 ms animation covers 18 frames. At 2 frames per second only one frame of the 30 is sampled, and it falls before the animation starts.
hero.strip_note: A 300 ms animation at 60 fps spans 18 frames. Sampling 2 frames per second catches 0 or 1 of them.

features.title: What it does
features.motion_body: Start, duration, easing as cubic-bezier, stagger and travel of each animated element, to the frame, written out as CSS.
features.content_body: Scene cuts, keyframes, Korean and English on-screen text (macOS Vision), a speech transcript and audio/video sync.
features.local_body: ffmpeg, OpenCV, macOS Vision, Apple on-device speech recognition and whisper.cpp. Video and audio stay on your Mac.

example.title: Example: a 3-second toast recording
example.body: The toast was rendered from real CSS in headless Chrome, so the right answer is known.

why.title: Why
why.watch_intro: /watch (claude-video 0.1.3) is built for a quick look at what a video is about. video-use edits videos by conversation: cuts, colour and subtitles. video-lens is for when something happens, for how long and how.
why.row_frames_watch: At most 2 per second, 100 in total
why.row_frames_video_use: 10 frames per requested range, 320 px wide, when it asks for them
why.row_precision_video_use: Word timestamps for speech; frames at the times it asks for
why.row_anim_video_use: Only the frames it samples; motion is not measured
why.row_anim_lens: Start, duration, easing and CSS measured
why.row_speech_watch: Audio uploaded to Groq or OpenAI Whisper unless English captions exist
why.row_speech_video_use: Audio uploaded to ElevenLabs Scribe (paid API key)
why.row_speech_lens: Transcribed on your Mac, Korean included
why.row_scenes_lens: Cut times and the text of each slide
why.lens_shaded: Shaded: what video-lens does that the other two do not.
why.watch_measured: In the benchmark, Opus with /watch or video-use scored a little higher on average than with video-lens, mostly because it measured the clip itself with its own ffmpeg and OpenCV code on top of the skill, and it cost more than twice as much. Details: [Against other video skills](#skills-compare).
why.alone_body: Without the skill, Claude writes new ffmpeg and Python code for each video and measures with it. That often works, but the code differs every run.
why.alone_spread: Task "{task}": {model} alone had a median score of {median} over {reps} runs and {worst} in its worst run.
why.alone_after: video-lens runs one tested pipeline instead, so every run starts from the same measurements.
why.alone_model: {model}: cost {cost}, time {time}, mean score {skill_mean} against {base_mean}, worst run {skill_worst} against {base_worst}.

bench.title: Benchmarks
bench.intro: {tasks} tasks scored against answer keys, {reps} runs each, so {runs} runs per condition, measured from {from} to {date}. Each model ran alone (writing its own ffmpeg and Python) and with video-lens, with the same prompt, no MCP servers and one run at a time. The tool and effort level each model ran with are under [How we measured](#method).
bench.close_scores: Both conditions solve most tasks, so mean scores sit close together. The worst run shows how far a single run can go wrong.
bench.grok_time: Grok 4.7's time with video-lens is rough: those runs shared the Mac with other heavy work for part of the pass, and one of them took 4.3 hours. Its median time was 446 s against 778 s alone.
bench.autotrigger: Skill runs named the skill in the prompt. In a separate test where the prompt did not name it, Opus 5.5 chose it on its own in 8 of 9 tasks.
bench.method_link: How the tasks were built and scored: [How we measured](#method) and [BENCHMARK.md](https://github.com/Junhan2/video-lens/blob/main/docs/BENCHMARK.md).

note.watch: /watch ({version}) looks at up to 2 frames per second and sends speech to the Groq or OpenAI Whisper API.
note.video-use: video-use ({version}) is built to edit videos, not to measure them. It sends speech to ElevenLabs Scribe and looks at filmstrips of frames. These tasks test only how well it reads a video.

skills.own_note: Own analysis code: runs in which Opus also wrote and ran its own ffmpeg, OpenCV or whisper commands besides the skill's tools. Most /watch and video-use runs did, which is where their extra cost and time went. With video-lens the skill's measurements were usually enough.

when.title: When to use it
when.use_motion: **Rebuilding or reviewing UI motion.** Start, duration, easing and stagger as numbers and CSS, each with the range it could fall in. Questions such as "is this transition really 400 ms ease-out?" get a measured answer.
when.use_long: On the 10-minute Korean lecture, {model} with video-lens: cost {cost}, time {time} (median of {reps} runs).
when.use_repeat: **Repeated motion.** Carousels and loops are measured once as a group, with each repeat's start time.
when.use_private: **Private talks and meetings.** Speech is transcribed on your Mac, and slide text comes with timestamps.
when.skip_title: You do not need it for
when.skip_gist: **A quick gist of a short clip.** The model alone handles it, and loading the skill adds a little cost.
when.skip_os: **Windows or Linux.** video-lens runs on macOS only.
when.skip_features: **Speaker labels, language detection or music tempo.** These are not supported.

cases.title: Use case: rebuilding viral showreels
cases.intro: In the launch week of Claude Opus 5.5, a one-line prompt for a 15-second motion graphics showreel spread across X. We took {count} of the most-shared reels, one of them GPT-6 Astra's answer to the same prompt, and gave each to {model} in Claude Code with video-lens and a single prompt: work out how the video moves and rebuild it as one HTML page. Below is what came back, rendered frame by frame and left as it was, scored against its original.
cases.original: Original: [{author} on X]({url}), {likes} likes and {views} views
cases.look: **Looks alike:** {look} (two different reels from the trend: {floor})
cases.cuts: **Cuts:** {matched} of the original's {total} hard cuts are in the rebuild, within 0.1 s
cases.words: **Words:** {found} of the {total} words on screen in the original are in the rebuild
cases.run: **Run:** {minutes} min, {cost} at API prices, no human edits
cases.page_link: [Open the rebuilt page]({page}) (one HTML file that plays once when it opens)
cases.scoring_look: **Looks alike** is SSIM, a standard image similarity score, between the original and the rebuild at the same moment, 10 times a second (1 = identical). Two different reels from the same trend give the floor shown next to it.
cases.scoring_cuts: **Cuts** are found by ffmpeg's scene detector in both clips. A cut counts when the rebuild cuts within 0.1 s of the original.
cases.scoring_words: **Words** are read by the video-lens OCR in both clips, counting only dictionary words so misreadings drop out.
cases.scoring_originals: The originals stay on X: this page links to them and shows only the rebuilds, which are code Claude wrote. Likes and views are from [Revid's gallery of launch-week videos](https://www.revid.ai/claude-motion-graphics) on September 28, 2026. Scripts: [bench/cases](https://github.com/Junhan2/video-lens/tree/main/bench/cases).
cases.prompt_title: The prompt, the same for every reel except the render length (15.03 s for GPT-6 Astra's reel)

note.stephanlivera: Still off: the motion blur and RGB split are imitated with blur filters, the 3D dot shapes have no lines between the dots, and the width wobble on CLAUDE is weaker than in the original. The page asks for SF Pro and JetBrains Mono, so a browser without them shows other fonts; the video is the reference.
note.ajith: Still off: the dot sphere on cream is flatter than the original's spiky one, the red square outline above the blue floor at 7.35 s is missing, and film grain and motion blur were left out. The fonts are stand-ins that ship with macOS. Most of the missed words are pieces of text bent into a circle, which the OCR reads in fragments.
note.astra: Original: GPT-6 Astra's half of a side-by-side post, cut at the frame where its reel starts (16.8 s). Still off: the chrome 3D objects (knot, ribbon, figure eight, star) are flat SVG and CSS stand-ins without the reflections, and the headline font differs. This reel changes scenes mostly with wipes, which the hard-cut count does not include; by the run's own measurement, 6 of its 7 transitions land on the same frame as the original's and one is a frame late.

install.title: Install
install.req_macos: macOS. Tested on macOS 26 with Apple Silicon.
install.req_python: Python 3 with opencv-python and numpy. Tested with Python 3.13. If a package is missing, the skill prints the exact pip command.
install.req_xcode: Xcode Command Line Tools, to build the on-screen text and speech helpers.
install.opt_speech: macOS 26 for on-device speech recognition (Apple SpeechTranscriber).
install.opt_whisper: whisper-cpp and a ggml model (for example `ggml-large-v3-turbo-q5_0.bin`) in `~/.local/share/whisper/`, to transcribe with whisper.
install.opt_chrome: Node 24 and Google Chrome, to read a web page's declared CSS animations and compare them with the measurement.
install.opt_ytdlp: yt-dlp, to analyse a video from a URL.

usage.title: Usage
usage.body: Ask as usual. Claude picks the skill when a question needs measuring. To call it directly, start your message with `/video-lens`.
usage.ex_motion: Analyse the animation in this screen recording so I can rebuild it in CSS
usage.ex_slides: List when each slide appears in this lecture and what it says
usage.ex_digest: Summarise this YouTube talk scene by scene with screenshots
usage.tip: When several elements move at once, name the area, for example "only the list on the left". Claude then narrows the measurement with `--roi`.
usage.digest_title: Scene digest, only when you ask
usage.digest_body: Ask for a scene-by-scene summary with screenshots and Claude writes `digest.md` and a self-contained `digest.html`: one capture per scene, one or two lines on what happens, what was said, and a link to that moment. A YouTube video with chapters is split by its chapters. On a 66-minute Korean talk with 21 chapters this took about 4 minutes on the Mac (download, analysis and digest). Ordinary analyses never make one.

how.title: How it works
how.intro: One command, `vl.py analyze`, measures the video and prints a text report of at most 6,000 characters. Claude reads that first, then a few labelled images, and single frames only when needed.
how.s1_body: ffprobe reads the streams, the frame rate and each frame's timestamp, so variable frame rate recordings keep their real timing.
how.s2_body: Sound activity and onsets. A quiet clip of up to 2 minutes goes to motion mode, a longer one to content mode, a short clip with sound gets both.
how.s3_body: Captions or an on-device transcript (Apple SpeechTranscriber or whisper.cpp), scene cuts, keyframes and on-screen text with macOS Vision.
how.s4_body: OpenCV finds the moving elements and tracks them frame by frame. Start, duration, easing (a named curve or cubic-bezier), stagger and travel are fitted and written as CSS.
how.s5_body: The offset between sound and picture, from paired onsets.
how.s6_body: A text report with ranges and confidence, a timeline, and labelled contact sheets with timing maps.
how.reading: Reading order for Claude: report, then timeline or text search, then the overview image, then contact sheets, then single frames.

method.title: How we measured
method.keys: **Answer keys.** The UI tasks are real CSS animations rendered frame by frame in headless Chrome, so the truth is the CSS as written. The lectures are narrated with macOS text-to-speech. The carousel is a real screen recording with an approximate key.
method.same: **Same conditions.** Same prompt, model and effort in both conditions, no MCP servers, one run at a time. Skill runs start the prompt with the skill's name (`/video-lens` in Claude Code). Each prompt asks for a JSON answer in a fixed format that a script scores against the key.
method.hidden: **Skill hidden from the baseline.** Baseline runs load no skills and cannot read the skill's folder. This was added after an early baseline run found video-lens on disk and ran it.
method.score: **Score.** Each answer is checked item by item against the key. A run's score is the checks passed minus false positives, divided by the number of checks, never below 0.
method.tolerance: **Tolerances.** Start and duration within ±1 frame, easing within 0.05 of the true curve, sounds within ±10 ms, speech timing within ±150 ms.
method.more: Full method, per-task numbers and caveats: [BENCHMARK.md](https://github.com/Junhan2/video-lens/blob/main/docs/BENCHMARK.md). Scripts to reproduce the runs: [bench/](https://github.com/Junhan2/video-lens/blob/main/bench/README.md).

limits.title: Limits
limits.merge: Several elements moving at once can come out merged into one box or split into fragments in the first pass. Narrowing the area with `--roi` fixes it. In the benchmark Opus 5.5 did this on its own; Sonnet 5.5 did it less often.
limits.backgrounds: Motion over photo or gradient backgrounds and noisy real-world speech are under-tested.
limits.features: No speaker labels, language auto-detection or music tempo.
limits.fps: 30 fps recordings halve the timing resolution. Record at 60 fps when you can.
limits.os: macOS only, tested on macOS 26 with Apple Silicon.
